Derived values are computed without synchronization effects.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the revised tested form showing loading, success, and recovery states with an annotated React render trace.
rubric: Level 1: Form state is duplicated or an effect still synchronizes derived React state.
Level 2: The render trace assigns one owner and shows loading, success, and recovery after each event.
Level 3: The diagnosis also predicts and tests one stale-render or duplicate-submit failure.

templates.title: Rehearse state, events and effects
templates.objective: Classify logic as event handling, render derivation, or external synchronization.
templates.whyNow: Fast classification prevents effects from becoming a general-purpose control-flow tool.

steps.label: Refactor three logic fragments into their correct React locations

templates.buildTask: Refactor a tested form with loading, success, and recovery states: place event, derived, and synchronization logic correctly.
completionCriteria: User-triggered work occurs in event handlers.
Effects synchronize only with an external system.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the refactored tested form with loading, success, and recovery states and a state-event-effect rationale.
rubric: Level 1: React event work, render derivation, and effects remain mixed or the form cannot retry.
Level 2: The form exposes loading and success while recovery is driven by a clear user event.
Level 3: The rationale also proves effects touch only external systems and tests the recovery boundary.

templates.title: Author a keyboard-safe component state model
templates.objective: Define and implement interaction states with semantic roles, keyboard behavior, focus visibility, and error relationships.
templates.whyNow: Reusable components amplify both accessibility strengths and defects across a product.

steps.label: Specify component states and keyboard transitions
Implement focus, contrast, and error relationships

templates.buildTask: Build a reusable component with visible focus and state text: add keyboard-safe input and programmatic error relationships.
completionCriteria: Keyboard behavior and focus order match the state contract.
Error and disabled states remain perceivable without color alone.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the reusable component with visible focus and state text, its state model, and keyboard test record.
rubric: Level 1: The component loses keyboard focus, hides a state in color, or disconnects error text.
Level 2: The reusable component follows its state model with visible focus and explicit state text.
Level 3: Tests also cover disabled, invalid, and recovery transitions without focus loss.

templates.title: Audit semantics, focus and contrast
templates.objective: Audit one component for semantic role, accessible name, focus indication, and state contrast.
templates.whyNow: A short evidence-based audit exposes systemic component defects early.

steps.label: Run and record a semantics, focus, and contrast audit

templates.buildTask: Audit a reusable component with visible focus and state text: prioritize fixes for semantics, keyboard behavior, and contrast.
completionCriteria: The audit records pass/fail evidence for every check.
Each proposed fix maps to an observed defect.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the audit and repaired reusable component with visible focus and state text plus contrast evidence.
rubric: Level 1: The component audit lacks evidence for semantics, keyboard focus, contrast, or state text.
Level 2: Each component finding has observed evidence and the repair restores visible focus and state text.
Level 3: The audit also prioritizes systemic token or semantic fixes and verifies no regression.

templates.title: Rebuild focus and error relationships
templates.objective: Repair focus indicators and accessible error descriptions in an existing field component.
templates.whyNow: Repeated repair builds fluency with the relationships users depend on.

steps.label: Repair focus and error semantics and verify by keyboard

templates.buildTask: Rebuild a reusable component with visible focus and state text: restore invalid-state and error-description relationships.
completionCriteria: Focus remains visible in every interactive state.
The error text is programmatically associated and announced.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the revised reusable component with visible focus and state text plus keyboard verification.
rubric: Level 1: The component focus indicator disappears or error state text is not programmatically related.
Level 2: Visible focus persists and the reusable component announces specific error state text.
Level 3: Keyboard verification also covers focus recovery after the error is corrected.

templates.title: Design a typed idempotent write endpoint
templates.objective: Specify a write endpoint with validated input, idempotency behavior, safe errors, and stable response types.
templates.whyNow: Explicit write semantics prevent duplicate effects and ambiguous client recovery.

steps.label: Specify request, response, and idempotency contract
Implement and exercise safe success and failure cases

templates.buildTask: Implement a request/response contract with safe error cases: add typed idempotent write behavior and repeated-request evidence.
completionCriteria: Repeating the same idempotency key does not duplicate the write.
Validation, conflict, authorization, and server failures have distinct safe responses.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the request and response contract with safe error cases and repeated-write endpoint test evidence.
rubric: Level 1: The endpoint contract permits duplicate writes or exposes ambiguous HTTP error responses.
Level 2: The request-response contract proves idempotency and distinct safe error cases.
Level 3: Tests also cover concurrent retries and explain terminal versus retryable status semantics.

templates.title: Review an HTTP failure contract
templates.objective: Review status, body, retry, and disclosure behavior for each endpoint failure mode.
templates.whyNow: Clients can recover safely only when failure semantics are deliberate and stable.

steps.label: Classify and repair an endpoint failure matrix

templates.buildTask: Review a request/response contract with safe error cases: create a failure matrix and repair one ambiguous HTTP response.
completionCriteria: Each failure maps to a justified status and stable body.
Retryable and terminal failures are explicitly distinguished.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the HTTP request and response contract with safe error cases, failure matrix, and endpoint diff.
rubric: Level 1: The HTTP failure matrix leaves a request status, response body, or retry decision ambiguous.
Level 2: The contract assigns each failure a stable response and safe error disclosure.
Level 3: The review also tests one client retry boundary and prevents an unsafe repeated effect.

templates.title: Rehearse methods, status and retry semantics
templates.objective: Choose HTTP methods, statuses, and retry behavior for concrete request scenarios.
templates.whyNow: Fast semantic choices keep APIs consistent under delivery pressure.

steps.label: Resolve method, status, and retry cases with rationale

templates.buildTask: Rehearse a request/response contract with safe error cases: decide methods, statuses, and retries for five endpoint cases.
completionCriteria: Every method and status matches the stated semantics.
Retry guidance avoids repeating unsafe effects.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the completed HTTP request and response contract table with methods, statuses, retries, and safe error cases.
rubric: Level 1: A request method, response status, or retry choice conflicts with the stated operation.
Level 2: The contract table gives correct HTTP semantics and safe errors for every case.
Level 3: The table also distinguishes idempotent recovery from conflict resolution with evidence.

templates.title: Ship a Worker-compatible route boundary
templates.objective: Implement an edge handler using Web APIs and injected bindings without importing Node-only capabilities.
templates.whyNow: Runtime portability must be enforced at the route boundary before deployment.

steps.label: Define binding interfaces and implement the Web API handler
Test runtime isolation and scan for Node-only leakage

templates.buildTask: Build an edge handler with injected bindings and no Node-only leak: use Web-standard request handling and isolate-local state.
completionCriteria: The handler depends on an explicit environment interface.
A focused test and import review show no Node-only runtime dependency.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the edge handler with injected bindings, no Node-only leak, and its test/build report.
rubric: Level 1: The edge handler imports a Node-only API or reads an undeclared ambient binding.
Level 2: The handler uses Web APIs and injected bindings with no Node-only leak.
Level 3: Isolation tests also prove request-local state and portable failure handling.

templates.title: Explain edge constraints and bindings
templates.objective: Explain isolate lifetime, binding injection, Web API availability, and state boundaries.
templates.whyNow: A correct mental model prevents accidental process-global and Node-specific designs.

steps.label: Annotate an edge route against isolate and binding constraints

templates.buildTask: Review an edge handler with injected bindings and no Node-only leak: classify runtime-safe, binding-dependent, and incompatible operations.
completionCriteria: Binding access is separated from business logic.
The review identifies isolate-lifetime and compatibility risks.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the annotated edge handler review showing injected bindings and every Node-only leak check.
rubric: Level 1: The edge review confuses isolate lifetime, injected bindings, or Node-only compatibility.
Level 2: The handler annotation locates each binding and rules out Node-only leakage.
Level 3: The review also predicts a process-global failure and proposes an isolate-safe test.

templates.title: Rebuild the isolate execution model
templates.objective: Refactor a process-oriented handler into an isolate-safe request lifecycle.
templates.whyNow: Practice exposes assumptions about persistent memory and ambient environment access.

steps.label: Remove persistent-process assumptions from a route

templates.buildTask: Rebuild an edge handler with injected bindings and no Node-only leak: localize request state and declare every capability.
completionCriteria: No correctness depends on mutable process-global state.
All external services are accessed through declared bindings.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the refactored edge handler with injected bindings, no Node-only leak, and isolate-safety evidence.
rubric: Level 1: The edge handler still depends on persistent memory or ambient runtime capabilities.
Level 2: Request state is local, bindings are injected, and no Node-only leak remains.
Level 3: Verification also exercises consecutive isolates and a binding failure boundary.

templates.title: Model immutable versions and relations
templates.objective: Design additive version tables, ownership relations, keys, and explicit delete behavior.
templates.whyNow: Historical planning data stays trustworthy only when versions and ownership are modeled explicitly.

steps.label: Model entities, immutable versions, keys, and ownership
Add constraints and exercise relation and delete cases

templates.buildTask: Create an additive relational schema with ownership boundaries: model immutable versions, keys, relations, and delete behavior.
completionCriteria: Keys and foreign keys enforce the intended cardinality.
Update and delete behavior preserves retained historical versions.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the additive relational schema with ownership boundaries and tests for valid, conflicting, and delete cases.
rubric: Level 1: The relational schema permits mutable history, orphaned rows, or cross-owner relations.
Level 2: Additive versions, keys, and ownership boundaries enforce intended cardinality.
Level 3: SQL tests also prove retention under delete actions and reject ownership conflicts.

templates.title: Review keys, cardinality and delete actions
templates.objective: Review a schema for missing uniqueness, incorrect cardinality, and unsafe referential actions.
templates.whyNow: Small relational mistakes become expensive data-integrity failures after launch.

steps.label: Audit keys, cardinality, and delete actions

templates.buildTask: Audit an additive relational schema with ownership boundaries: propose minimal key, cardinality, and delete corrections.
completionCriteria: Every relationship has stated cardinality and ownership.
Delete actions have an explicit retention rationale.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the annotated additive relational schema with ownership boundaries and proposed key/delete constraint diff.
rubric: Level 1: The schema audit leaves a key, relationship cardinality, delete action, or owner ambiguous.
Level 2: The relational schema annotation identifies enforceable ownership boundaries and exact fixes.
Level 3: The audit also supplies SQL cases that fail before each integrity constraint is added.

templates.title: Rehearse joins and integrity constraints
templates.objective: Write joins and constraints that preserve tenant ownership and relational invariants.
templates.whyNow: Repeated boundary cases build fluency beyond happy-path queries.

steps.label: Write ownership-safe joins and constraint cases

templates.buildTask: Rehearse an additive relational schema with ownership boundaries: implement one safe join and two integrity constraints.
completionCriteria: The join cannot cross ownership boundaries.
Invalid parent and duplicate relation cases are rejected.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the additive relational schema with ownership boundaries plus recorded join and constraint results.
rubric: Level 1: The SQL join crosses ownership or a missing constraint accepts an invalid relation.
Level 2: The relational schema and query enforce ownership boundaries and integrity constraints.
Level 3: Results also explain query shape and prove duplicate and missing-parent failures.

templates.title: Design private object metadata and compensation
templates.objective: Design private object keys, authoritative metadata, and compensation for partial put or delete failures.
templates.whyNow: Object and database operations lack a shared transaction and require deliberate recovery.

steps.label: Specify private keys, metadata ownership, and access checks
Model put, get, cleanup, and compensation outcomes

templates.buildTask: Author a put/get/cleanup sequence with private object keys: add owner-scoped metadata and explicit compensation.
completionCriteria: Object keys are unguessable and never grant authorization by themselves.
Every partial failure has an observable recovery or cleanup path.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the put, get, and cleanup sequence with private object keys and its failure-case table.
rubric: Level 1: The object sequence exposes guessable keys or omits cleanup after a partial put.
Level 2: Put, get, and cleanup use private object keys with owner-scoped metadata.
Level 3: The sequence also proves compensation for database and object-storage failure ordering.

templates.title: Threat-model an object access path
templates.objective: Trace authorization, metadata lookup, object access, and response disclosure for one object request.
templates.whyNow: Private buckets do not replace application-level ownership checks.

steps.label: Threat-model an object read and its failure paths

templates.buildTask: Threat-model a put/get/cleanup sequence with private object keys: trace authorization, disclosure, and compensation risks.
completionCriteria: Authentication and object ownership checks are separate gates.
Existence and metadata are not leaked to unauthorized callers.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the threat model and a put, get, and cleanup sequence using private object keys.
rubric: Level 1: The object threat model treats possession of a key as authorization or leaks metadata.
Level 2: The put-get-cleanup sequence gates private object keys behind ownership checks.
Level 3: Abuse cases also cover stale metadata, partial deletion, and existence disclosure.

templates.title: Rehearse database-versus-object boundaries
templates.objective: Assign authority correctly between relational metadata and immutable object bytes.
templates.whyNow: Clear authority prevents orphaned objects and access decisions based on storage keys.

steps.label: Classify metadata, bytes, ownership, and cleanup responsibilities

templates.buildTask: Rehearse a put/get/cleanup sequence with private object keys: assign database, byte-storage, ownership, and cleanup authority.
completionCriteria: The database remains authoritative for ownership and lifecycle state.
Object storage contains bytes addressed only after authorization.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the database/object boundary table and put, get, and cleanup sequence with private object keys.
rubric: Level 1: The object boundary table assigns ownership authority to a storage key or omits cleanup.
Level 2: Database metadata controls private object-key access across put, get, and cleanup.
Level 3: The table also resolves replace and orphan-recovery failures without unsafe access.

templates.title: Drive one behavior from RED to GREEN
templates.objective: Write a focused behavior test, observe the intended failure, implement the minimum fix, and retain both outputs.
templates.whyNow: A witnessed RED proves the test detects the missing behavior before GREEN earns confidence.

steps.label: Specify behavior and capture the meaningful RED failure
Implement minimally and capture focused GREEN

templates.buildTask: Create a focused test proving a meaningful failure before implementation: drive one behavior from RED to minimal GREEN.
completionCriteria: The RED output fails for the missing behavior rather than setup error.
The focused test passes after implementation without weakening assertions.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the focused test proving a meaningful failure before implementation plus the commit and RED/GREEN output.
rubric: Level 1: The focused test errors in setup or passes before the behavior implementation.
Level 2: The test captures a meaningful RED failure, then passes unchanged after minimal implementation.
Level 3: A targeted mutation also fails at the behavioral assertion and the commit remains focused.

templates.title: Strengthen a weak regression test
templates.objective: Replace implementation-coupled assertions with an observable behavior and meaningful failure case.
templates.whyNow: Weak tests can stay green while user-visible behavior breaks.

steps.label: Diagnose and strengthen one regression test

templates.buildTask: Strengthen a focused test proving a meaningful failure before implementation: replace weak assertions and exercise a realistic mutation.
completionCriteria: Assertions observe public behavior rather than private calls.
A targeted mutation produces the expected failure.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the focused test proving a meaningful failure before implementation and mutation RED evidence.
rubric: Level 1: The regression test asserts private calls or survives the defect mutation.
Level 2: The focused test observes public behavior and proves a meaningful RED failure before implementation.
Level 3: Boundary cases also discriminate two plausible regressions without brittle assertions.

templates.title: Rehearse boundary and mutation tests
templates.objective: Choose boundary cases and mutations that discriminate correct behavior from plausible defects.
templates.whyNow: Short mutation practice reveals assertions that do not protect the contract.

steps.label: Add one boundary case and prove one mutation is caught

templates.buildTask: Rehearse a focused test proving a meaningful failure before implementation: add one contract boundary and discriminating mutation.
completionCriteria: The boundary is derived from the public contract.
The mutation fails at the intended assertion.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the focused test proving a meaningful failure before implementation and its boundary/mutation report.
rubric: Level 1: The test boundary is arbitrary or the mutation does not produce the expected failure.
Level 2: The focused test catches a contract boundary and records RED before implementation.
Level 3: The mutation report also explains why the assertion distinguishes the intended behavior.

templates.title: Enforce session, ownership and secret boundaries
templates.objective: Enforce authentication, owner-scoped authorization, safe failures, and server-only secret access on one route.
templates.whyNow: Authenticated access is not authorized access, and boundary mistakes expose other users or credentials.

steps.label: Threat-model session, ownership, and secret boundaries
Implement owner-scoped checks and negative tests

templates.buildTask: Produce a threat model plus owner-scoped negative tests: enforce session, secret, anonymous, and cross-owner route boundaries.
completionCriteria: Authentication and ownership are checked independently before data access.
Secrets remain server-only and failure responses disclose no protected state.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the threat model plus owner-scoped negative tests for anonymous, wrong-owner, and secret-boundary cases.
rubric: Level 1: The threat model merges session authentication with ownership authorization or exposes a secret.
Level 2: Owner-scoped negative tests reject anonymous and cross-owner access before protected data reads.
Level 3: Tests also prove safe response disclosure and server-only secret handling across failure paths.

templates.title: Audit one authorization path
templates.objective: Audit one request from session validation through owner-scoped data access and response shaping.
templates.whyNow: Authorization defects often hide between individually reasonable layers.

steps.label: Trace and test one authorization decision path

templates.buildTask: Audit a threat model plus owner-scoped negative tests: repair the highest-risk authorization gap and add missing denial cases.
completionCriteria: Every protected read or write is constrained by owner identity.
Anonymous, wrong-owner, and missing-record outcomes are tested safely.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the authorization threat model, repair diff, and owner-scoped negative tests for the audited path.
rubric: Level 1: The authorization audit omits an ownership gate or lacks a cross-owner negative test.
Level 2: The threat model traces session identity to owner-scoped access and safe rejection.
Level 3: Negative tests also cover missing records and demonstrate non-disclosing responses.

templates.title: Separate authentication from authorization
templates.objective: Distinguish identity proof from permission checks in concrete access decisions.
templates.whyNow: The distinction prevents logged-in users from inheriting unintended access.

steps.label: Classify and repair authentication and authorization checks

templates.buildTask: Rehearse a threat model plus owner-scoped negative tests: separate identity and permission gates and add a cross-owner case.
completionCriteria: Authentication establishes identity only.
Authorization binds the requested resource to that identity.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the authentication/authorization threat model and owner-scoped negative tests including a cross-owner request.
rubric: Level 1: The route treats an authenticated session as sufficient authorization.
Level 2: Owner-scoped negative tests prove the separate identity and permission gates.
Level 3: The threat model also identifies secret, enumeration, and stale-session failure boundaries.

templates.title: Build a reversible delivery runbook
templates.objective: Author a delivery sequence with build gates, smoke checks, migration safety, observability, and rollback triggers.
templates.whyNow: A release is safe only when failure can be detected and reversed deliberately.

steps.label: Define build, configuration, and pre-release gates
Specify smoke checks, rollback triggers, and recovery

templates.buildTask: Create a build, smoke-check, and rollback checklist: define reversible gates, owners, triggers, and recovery for one release.
completionCriteria: Every release gate has an owner and observable pass condition.
Rollback triggers, steps, and data compatibility are explicit.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the build, smoke-check, and rollback checklist with a dry-run record.
rubric: Level 1: The delivery runbook lacks a build gate, smoke-check, rollback trigger, or owner.
Level 2: The checklist makes build, smoke-check, and rollback steps executable and observable.
Level 3: The dry run also validates data compatibility and a timed rollback decision.

templates.title: Diagnose a failed build or release
templates.objective: Use build and release evidence to isolate a failure stage and select a safe recovery action.
templates.whyNow: Fast diagnosis must preserve recoverability rather than compound a failed release.

steps.label: Diagnose a release failure and choose rollback or fix-forward

templates.buildTask: Diagnose a build, smoke-check, and rollback checklist: identify the first failed gate and choose evidence-backed recovery.
completionCriteria: The diagnosis identifies the first failed gate.
The recovery choice accounts for data and version compatibility.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the failed-release diagnosis and its repaired build, smoke-check, and rollback checklist.
rubric: Level 1: The diagnosis guesses beyond evidence or selects recovery before finding the failed build gate.
Level 2: The smoke-check evidence identifies the failure and the rollback checklist gives a safe response.
Level 3: The decision also compares rollback with fix-forward under data-version constraints.

templates.title: Rehearse environment and rollback boundaries
templates.objective: Classify configuration, secrets, build artifacts, and data changes by environment and rollback behavior.
templates.whyNow: Boundary rehearsal prevents environment drift and incomplete rollback plans.

steps.label: Map environment inputs and rollback behavior

templates.buildTask: Rehearse a build, smoke-check, and rollback checklist: map environment inputs, stateful changes, and recovery boundaries.
completionCriteria: Secrets and public configuration have distinct handling.
Each stateful change has a compatible rollback or forward-recovery path.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the environment matrix and a build, smoke-check, and rollback checklist for the release.
rubric: Level 1: The environment matrix mixes secrets, public config, or stateful rollback assumptions.
Level 2: The checklist connects each build artifact to a smoke-check and rollback action.
Level 3: It also documents forward recovery for state that cannot be rolled back safely.

templates.title: Emit useful telemetry without private data
templates.objective: Design structured events, counters, and correlation fields that answer operational questions without sensitive payloads.
templates.whyNow: Telemetry is useful only when it supports diagnosis without becoming a privacy liability.

steps.label: Define operational questions and structured event fields
Add allowed counters and verify redaction

templates.buildTask: Author a structured event contract with allowed counters only: add bounded correlation fields and explicit redaction rules.
completionCriteria: Each signal answers a named operational question.
Secrets, content, and direct personal identifiers are excluded or redacted.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the structured event contract with allowed counters only plus redaction tests and example output.
rubric: Level 1: The telemetry event includes private data, unbounded labels, or counters without an operational question.
Level 2: The structured event contract emits allowed counters only and passes redaction tests.
Level 3: The signal design also demonstrates correlation and diagnosis without sensitive payloads.

templates.title: Audit signal quality and redaction
templates.objective: Evaluate whether existing signals are actionable, attributable, low-cardinality, and privacy-safe.
templates.whyNow: Noisy or unsafe telemetry increases cost while weakening incident response.

steps.label: Audit one event set for utility and redaction

templates.buildTask: Audit a structured event contract with allowed counters only: remove one unsafe field and one non-actionable signal.
completionCriteria: Every retained field has an operational purpose.
The audit records cardinality and privacy risk for each field.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the audited structured event contract with allowed counters only and before/after redaction evidence.
rubric: Level 1: The signal audit retains a private field, high-cardinality label, or unactionable event.
Level 2: The structured event contract keeps allowed counters only and records each redaction decision.
Level 3: The audit also proves the retained telemetry answers a named incident question.

templates.title: Rehearse metrics, logs and traces
templates.objective: Select the appropriate signal type for counts, event details, and cross-boundary latency.
templates.whyNow: Correct signal selection reduces noise and shortens diagnosis.

steps.label: Map operational questions to metrics, logs, and traces

templates.buildTask: Rehearse a structured event contract with allowed counters only: map four production questions to bounded signals.
completionCriteria: Each question maps to the least costly sufficient signal.
Labels and correlation fields have bounded cardinality.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the signal table and resulting structured event contract with allowed counters only.
rubric: Level 1: Metrics, logs, or traces are chosen without regard to event detail, latency, or cardinality.
Level 2: The structured event contract uses allowed counters only and maps each signal to a question.
Level 3: The table also sets bounded labels, correlation fields, and privacy-safe retention.

templates.title: Validate a mocked structured-model boundary
templates.objective: Build a provider-independent schema gate that accepts valid structured output and rejects malformed mocked fixtures.
templates.whyNow: Model output is untrusted input even when a provider advertises structured generation.

steps.label: Define the provider-independent output contract
Exercise malformed, partial, and valid mocked outputs

templates.buildTask: Implement a provider-independent schema gate with malformed fixtures: accept valid mocked output and reject unsafe variants.
completionCriteria: Application code receives only schema-validated values.
Malformed, missing, and unexpected fields follow a safe typed failure path.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the provider-independent schema gate with malformed fixtures and the focused mocked-output test report.
rubric: Level 1: Model output reaches domain logic without schema validation or malformed fixtures are accepted.
Level 2: The provider-independent schema gate accepts valid output and safely rejects every malformed fixture.
Level 3: Tests also prove unknown fields, partial output, and provider adapter changes cannot bypass the gate.

templates.title: Reject malformed model output safely
templates.objective: Diagnose and close a model-output path that trusts parsing, markdown, or partial structure.
templates.whyNow: One permissive path can bypass otherwise strong application contracts.

steps.label: Repair and test one malformed-output boundary

templates.buildTask: Repair a provider-independent schema gate with malformed fixtures: replace unsafe model-output assumptions with typed failures.
completionCriteria: Invalid structure never reaches domain logic.
The failure path is deterministic and excludes raw provider content.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the repaired provider-independent schema gate with malformed fixtures and safe-failure test evidence.
rubric: Level 1: The model boundary still trusts parsed text, markdown, or partial output.
Level 2: The provider-independent schema gate rejects malformed fixtures without exposing provider content.
Level 3: The repair also records deterministic typed failures for missing and unexpected fields.

templates.title: Separate prompt text from output contracts
templates.objective: Separate changeable prompt instructions from stable validated domain output.
templates.whyNow: Prompt revisions should not silently redefine application data contracts.

steps.label: Refactor prompt and output responsibilities

templates.buildTask: Rehearse a provider-independent schema gate with malformed fixtures: separate prompt adapters from the stable output contract.
completionCriteria: The prompt contains no parsing contract relied on by domain code.
The same schema gate can validate output from another provider adapter.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the provider-independent schema gate with malformed fixtures plus the separated prompt adapter.
rubric: Level 1: Prompt text still defines output parsing behavior relied on by application code.
Level 2: The provider-independent schema gate rejects malformed fixtures independently of the prompt adapter.
Level 3: A second model adapter also passes the same output-contract tests without schema changes.

templates.title: Rank attributable evidence without fetching
templates.objective: Rank a supplied evidence set using relevance, authority, recency, coverage, and explicit attribution.
templates.whyNow: Useful retrieval depends on evidence quality and provenance, not merely similarity.

steps.label: Register supplied sources and define ranking evidence
Rank passages and justify attribution and exclusions

templates.buildTask: Build an evidence registry with explicit source-quality rationale: rank supplied passages without network fetching.
completionCriteria: Every ranked claim resolves to a registered source and passage.
Ranking rationale addresses relevance, authority, recency, and coverage.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the evidence registry with explicit source-quality rationale and deterministic ranking report.
rubric: Level 1: Ranked evidence lacks a resolvable source, passage, or provenance record.
Level 2: The evidence registry gives explicit source-quality rationale for relevance, authority, recency, and coverage.
Level 3: The ranking also labels conflicts and insufficient evidence without fetching or invention.

templates.title: Audit provenance, recency and coverage
templates.objective: Audit an evidence set for source identity, publication context, recency, and claim coverage.
templates.whyNow: Attribution can be present yet still fail to support the conclusion.

steps.label: Audit evidence provenance, recency, and coverage

templates.buildTask: Audit an evidence registry with explicit source-quality rationale: mark unsupported, stale, and weakly attributed claims.
completionCriteria: Each issue identifies the affected claim and source record.
The audit distinguishes missing evidence from low-quality evidence.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the audited evidence registry with explicit source-quality rationale for every flagged claim.
rubric: Level 1: The provenance audit flags evidence without tying it to a claim and source record.
Level 2: The evidence registry records explicit source-quality rationale for recency and coverage gaps.
Level 3: The audit also separates absent evidence, weak authority, and conflicting attribution.

templates.title: Rehearse source attribution decisions
templates.objective: Choose which source supports each claim and state when evidence is insufficient.
templates.whyNow: Short attribution practice resists confident synthesis beyond the supplied evidence.

steps.label: Map claims to supporting passages and gaps

templates.buildTask: Rehearse an evidence registry with explicit source-quality rationale: complete a claim-to-source matrix and label evidence gaps.
completionCriteria: Every supported claim identifies an exact source passage.
Unsupported or conflicting claims are labeled without invention.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the attribution matrix as an evidence registry with explicit source-quality rationale.
rubric: Level 1: A claim is attributed to no passage or to evidence that does not support it.
Level 2: The evidence registry maps each claim to a source and explicit source-quality rationale.
Level 3: The matrix also marks unsupported and conflicting claims without overstating coverage.

templates.title: Turn a user outcome into acceptance criteria
templates.objective: Define one product slice with a user outcome, non-goals, observable acceptance criteria, and release gates.
templates.whyNow: Outcome-centered scope connects technical work to a decision and prevents feature drift.

steps.label: Frame the user outcome, constraints, and non-goals
Write observable acceptance criteria and release gates

templates.buildTask: Create a one-page product slice with goals, non-goals, and gates: add observable acceptance criteria and outcome guardrails.
completionCriteria: The outcome describes a user change rather than a shipped feature.
Every criterion is observable and the non-goals constrain scope.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the one-page product slice with goals, non-goals, acceptance criteria, and gates.
rubric: Level 1: The product slice describes a feature output without a user outcome or bounded scope.
Level 2: The one-page product slice states goals, non-goals, observable criteria, and release gates.
Level 3: The slice also connects guardrails and decision evidence to the user outcome.

templates.title: Defend one scope trade-off
templates.objective: Compare two plausible scope choices and defend one using outcome, risk, effort, and reversibility.
templates.whyNow: Explicit trade-offs keep constrained delivery aligned with the highest-value learning.

steps.label: Evaluate and defend one scope trade-off

templates.buildTask: Defend a one-page product slice with goals, non-goals, and gates: choose between two scope options using shared evidence.

The chosen scope states what is deferred and how risk is contained.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the scope decision as a one-page product slice with goals, non-goals, and gates.
rubric: Level 1: The scope trade-off compares options with different criteria or hides deferred work.
Level 2: The one-page product slice defends goals, non-goals, and gates using shared evidence.
Level 3: The decision also addresses reversibility, outcome risk, and the next validation signal.

templates.title: Separate outcomes from feature output
templates.objective: Rewrite feature statements as observable user outcomes with guardrails.

steps.label: Rewrite feature outputs into outcome hypotheses

templates.buildTask: Rehearse a one-page product slice with goals, non-goals, and gates: convert three feature requests into outcome hypotheses.
completionCriteria: Each outcome names a user, behavior change, and observable signal.
Guardrails capture a plausible harmful side effect.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the outcome mapping as a one-page product slice with goals, non-goals, and gates.
rubric: Level 1: A feature statement remains an output without a user or observable outcome.

templates.title: Package a reviewable implementation artifact
templates.objective: Package a focused change with a clear claim, reproduction steps, verification evidence, and known limitations.
templates.whyNow: Inspectable proof lets another person evaluate capability without trusting a self-reported completion claim.

steps.label: Select and package the focused implementation artifact
Write reproduction, verification, and limitation notes

templates.buildTask: Package a commit or note with reproduction and verification evidence: tie every implementation claim to an exact artifact version.
completionCriteria: A reviewer can reproduce the claimed behavior from the instructions.
Evidence is tied to the exact artifact version and limitations are explicit.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the commit or note with reproduction steps and captured verification evidence.
rubric: Level 1: The implementation artifact claim has no exact commit, reproduction path, or fresh evidence.
Level 2: The commit or note lets a reviewer reproduce the behavior and inspect verification evidence.
Level 3: The package also states limitations and maps each claim to a precise artifact location.

templates.title: Assess whether a claim is inspectable
templates.objective: Assess whether a capability claim is supported by attributable, reproducible evidence.
templates.whyNow: A polished claim without inspectable proof cannot be independently evaluated.

steps.label: Audit one claim against its artifact and verification

templates.buildTask: Audit a commit or note with reproduction and verification evidence: identify gaps that prevent independent review.
completionCriteria: Every claim maps to a specific artifact location.
Reproduction steps and actual verification results are present.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the audited commit or note with reproduction steps, verification evidence, and identified gaps.
rubric: Level 1: A claim cannot be traced to a commit or note, reproduction step, and verification result.
Level 2: The audit links every inspectable claim to reproduction and verification evidence.
Level 3: It also narrows unsupported wording and distinguishes evidence gaps from implementation gaps.

templates.title: Rehearse claim-to-evidence mapping
templates.objective: Map implementation claims to exact artifacts, checks, and honest limitations.
templates.whyNow: Frequent mapping keeps evidence collection part of delivery rather than an afterthought.

steps.label: Build a claim-to-evidence map for one change

templates.buildTask: Rehearse a commit or note with reproduction and verification evidence: map claims to artifacts and remove unsupported wording.
completionCriteria: Each claim cites an exact artifact and verification check.
Unsupported claims are narrowed or labeled as limitations.
templates.proofRequirement: Provide the revised commit or note with reproduction steps, verification evidence, and claim mapping.
rubric: Level 1: The claim map cites a vague artifact or omits reproduction and verification evidence.
Level 2: Each claim resolves to a commit or note, exact reproduction step, and verification result.
Level 3: The mapping also records honest limitations and removes every unsupported completion claim.
